competition_series: FS UK (Silverstone) is their primary and best-documented competition; listed in the FSG team database but no evidence of regular FSG (Germany) driverless competition history was found.
summary: EUFS founded its whole-team organization in 2014 and formed a dedicated AI/driverless subteam around 2017, immediately targeting the brand-new DDT (Dynamic Driving Task) class at FSUK 2018 by using IMechE's shared, autonomous-systems-ready 'ADS-DV' platform rather than building their own vehicle - a choice that let them win the inaugural class in 2018 and every FS-AI class since (8 consecutive wins through 2025). In parallel, starting around 2020, EUFS began a much harder second track: building their own electric driverless car (ADS-EV/ADS class) from scratch, which is still not fully through scrutineering as of the March 2026 SISU26 launch. EUFS also built and open-sourced eufs_sim, a Gazebo-based FS driverless simulator that became the most widely forked/used open FS driverless sim in the ecosystem (hard-forked by QUT Motorsport, FSLART, and others). The team's own alumni material is candid that overall class dominance (via the loaner platform) masked much slower progress on individual dynamic events and on the self-built vehicle: EUFS reportedly took 4 years to first complete the skidpad event, and COVID-19 wiped out on-vehicle validation of an entire season's software (2020).
evidence_quality: moderate - strong on competition results and the DDT/ADS class distinction (multiple corroborating official/press sources), moderate-to-weak on hardware specifics (compute, EBS, steering actuator) which mix a first-hand 2020 alumni blog, a 2018 sponsor case study, and a 2024 sponsor press release that do not always agree with each other or clearly separate the loaner-ADS-DV era from the self-built ADS-EV era.
dv_program_start: [uncertain] ~2017 - EUFS's own history page frames 2017-2018 as 'entered the new DDT class'; a search-engine synthesis (not directly quoted from a primary page) states the AI/driverless subteam 'was started ... in 2017'. Whole-team EUFS was founded 2014.
first_autonomous_run_date: [uncertain] July 2018, at Silverstone during FSUK 2018 race week - per Mapix (30 Jul 2018): the software stack (built over '2 semesters' prior) was first run on the physical ADS-DV car during competition week, with only ~3 days to familiarize before the car 'completed a full lap on its first fully autonomous circuit attempt.' No earlier physical test date was found, meaning first-ever autonomous motion may have occurred at competition itself.
first_dv_competition: FSUK 2018 (Silverstone) - won the inaugural DDT (Dynamic Driving Task) class, the first Formula Student AI/driverless competition ever run in the UK.
months_concept_to_first_autonomous_run: [uncertain] approximately 12-18 months (subteam formed ~2017, first autonomous motion July 2018); exact month of formation not confirmed.
months_concept_to_first_competition: [uncertain] approximately 12-18 months (same window as above - the first competition entry and first autonomous run essentially coincided in 2018).
months_to_first_scoring_run: [uncertain] approximately 12-18 months - EUFS scored (won) dynamic DDT events at their very first competition entry in 2018, because the loaner ADS-DV platform removed vehicle-build risk from the schedule.

ramp_phases: Loaner-platform phase (~2017-2019): software-only development on IMechE's shared, pre-built 'ADS-DV' spec vehicle, with zero in-house vehicle engineering - enabled winning the DDT/FS-AI class in year 1 of competing. Own-vehicle phase (~2020-present, 6+ years and counting): building and integrating driverless onto an in-house-built electric car (ADS-EV/ADS class), progressing only incrementally through scrutineering (technical+safety in 2024, chassis+accumulator in 2025) and still not fully complete as of the 2026 SISU26 launch.
what_slipped: COVID-19 cancelled/virtualized FSUK dynamic events in 2020, so an entire season's software stack (FastSLAM2 + MPC) was, in the team's own words, never applied to the real car. The first self-built ADS-EV car (~2022) finished its powertrain on schedule but still failed scrutineering on debut. Winning the FS-AI/DDT class every year since 2018 masked much slower individual-event progress: EUFS reportedly took about 4 years to first complete the skidpad event even while winning the class outright on the loaner platform. Full ADS-vehicle scrutineering (safety+technical+chassis+accumulator all at once) was not achieved in one shot - it came piecewise across 2024 and 2025, with complete scrutineering still an explicit, unmet goal heading into FSUK 2026, i.e., roughly 6 years from ADS-EV program start to (hoped-for) full scrutineering pass on their own car.
platform_prerequisites: EUFS did NOT need to build (or convert) an EV before winning their first driverless competition, because IMechE's shared/purchased 'ADS-DV' spec platform arrives 'autonomous systems ready' and 'removes the requirement to design and manufacture a vehicle, leaving teams free to focus on developing their software' (per IMechE FS-AI FAQ). This is the single biggest reason EUFS could go from subteam formation (~2017) to winning the inaugural driverless class in year one (2018). Only later (~2020 onward) did EUFS attempt to build their own electric driverless car (ADS-EV) for the harder, from-scratch 'ADS' class - and that effort has taken 5-6+ years without yet being fully complete.
ebs_design: [uncertain] Not independently documented for EUFS specifically. EUFS's own site states only that the 'mechanical integration team ... manufacturing the emergency brake system design, then testing and improving it' (eufs.co/driverless), without disclosing architecture. Generic FS driverless EBS designs (which EUFS would need to satisfy DT.3.2) are electro-pneumatic systems using compressed air as passive stored energy, with a normally-open solenoid valve switching between armed/braked states and pneumatic-to-hydraulic intensifiers actuating the service brake calipers - but this is industry-generic, not confirmed as EUFS's specific implementation.
steering_actuation: [uncertain] Not confirmed as EUFS-specific. A commonly-cited FS driverless steering pattern (found via general search, not attributed to a named EUFS source) uses a rack-parallel ball screw driven by a brushless servo/DC motor, coupled to the steering rack via a cross-bore and shoulder screw, capable of lock-to-lock in ~0.4s and ~2000N at the rack - but no EUFS-specific document confirming this design was found.
sensor_mounting_packaging: [uncertain] Not documented with specifics. Mapix case study notes EUFS runs LiDAR and stereo camera as parallel, independent pipelines (for failover capability) rather than tightly fused, but does not describe exact mounting location on the vehicle.
mass_added: [uncertain] Not disclosed in any source found.
chassis_impact: [uncertain] Not documented; presumably required chassis/mounting modifications to convert the standard electric race car into the ADS-EV, but no specifics were found.
compute_platform: Cincoze DS-1202 industrial/rugged PC (per Steatite sponsorship announcement, tied to the 2024 FS-AI Class win), selected for robustness and resistance to temperature/shock/vibration/moisture/dust. Note: this is confirmed for the recent (2024-era) car; the 2018-era ADS-DV loaner platform's compute is not separately documented, and a 2020 first-hand blog does not name a specific onboard compute unit.
sensor_suite: Velodyne VLP-16 PUCK LiDAR (360° horizontal FOV, ~100m rated range, 16 channels, up to 600,000 pts/sec; Mapix has sponsored EUFS with this LiDAR since 2018); ZED / ZED2i stereo camera; GNSS/GPS; IMU; rear wheel speed sensors; steering angle sensor. Sourced from a combination of a 2018 sponsor case study, a 2020 first-hand team-member blog, and a later informatics.ed.ac.uk press release; exact sensor generation in use varies by year and is not perfectly reconciled across sources.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: [uncertain] Not documented with EUFS-specific detail; presumed to follow standard DT.4 shutdown-circuit integration (DS relay / remote-stop relay / EBS relay) common to all FS driverless entrants, but no EUFS-specific source confirms implementation.
custom_pcbs: [uncertain] EUFS's driverless team structure includes a dedicated 'PCB Design' role within Electrical (per eufs.co/driverless), implying custom PCBs are developed, but no specifics (which boards, design/fab/bring-up duration) were found.
software_stack: ROS-based (C++ primary language per a 2020 first-hand account), version-controlled on GitLab with CI/CD; eufs_sim (Gazebo-based, in-house-built and open-sourced) used as the core simulation environment for pre-vehicle validation.
ros_version: [uncertain] Originally ROS 1 (the original eufs_sim repository and a 2020 first-hand account both describe a ROS1-era stack); at least one hard fork (QUT-Motorsport/eufs_sim) is explicitly 'ROS2/Gazebo,' and the eufs_sim GitLab repo has separate 'ros1' branches, indicating an ROS1->ROS2 migration at some point, but the exact year EUFS's own competition stack switched is not confirmed.
perception_approach: 2020-era stack (per first-hand alumni blog): YOLOv3 neural network (custom-trained) for cone color/class detection, fused with LiDAR clustering via a Kalman filter. Per a 2018 Mapix case study, LiDAR (VLP-16) delivers accurate cone-location estimation to about 20m while the stereo camera pipeline is reliable to about 8-10m depth, run as a parallel/failover pipeline rather than tight fusion. A later informatics.ed.ac.uk release claims reliable cone detection 'at distances of up to 35m' - this figure is not reconciled with the Mapix 20m figure and may reflect a newer sensor generation or different measurement methodology [uncertain, conflicting sources].
slam_localization_approach: Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) based localization with FastSLAM2 for landmark SLAM (per 2020 first-hand alumni blog); described elsewhere in generic terms as 'algorithms [that] ensure precise navigation' without further technical detail on the official team site.
planning_approach: Elastic-band path optimization (per 2020 first-hand alumni blog), feeding into MPC for racing-speed laps.
control_approach: Model Predictive Control (MPC) used for racing-mode laps; a simpler look-ahead (pursuit-style) controller used for slower 'learning mode' exploration laps (per 2020 first-hand alumni blog).
simulation_tooling: eufs_sim - an in-house-built, open-source, Gazebo-based FS driverless simulator that models the perception pipeline from real-world data, simulates localization sensors, and uses a dynamic bicycle model for vehicle dynamics on FSUK-rule-compliant and randomly-generated tracks. It has become the most widely used/forked open FS driverless simulator in the ecosystem, with hard forks maintained by QUT-Motorsport and FSLART, among others.
ci_cd_testing: [uncertain] GitLab-integrated CI/CD is referenced (both by a 2020 first-hand blog and the official eufs.co/driverless page), but no detail on test suite composition, coverage, or HIL benches was found.
data_logging: [uncertain] Not documented with specifics; standard ROS-based teams typically use rosbag, but this was not confirmed for EUFS.
open_source_repos: gitlab.com/eufs/public/eufs_sim (primary, actively maintained simulator repo - very useful as a reference; it is the base for multiple other teams' driverless simulators, evidencing its quality/adoption); github.com/QUT-Motorsport/eufs_sim (ROS2/Gazebo hard fork, useful for seeing a ROS2 migration path); github.com/FSLART/eufs_sim (another hard fork); github.com/eufsa (EUFS Autonomous GitHub org, could not be fetched directly - access restricted at time of research).
critical_path_items: 1) Access to IMechE's shared 'ADS-DV' platform for the DDT/FS-AI class - this fully decoupled vehicle engineering from EUFS's early driverless timeline and was the single biggest enabler of their fast 2017-2018 ramp. 2) Completing and passing scrutineering on their own-built ADS-EV vehicle for the harder 'ADS' class - this has been the actual multi-year bottleneck (powertrain finished on time in 2022 but the car still failed scrutineering; full scrutineering still not achieved as of 2026). 3) COVID-19's cancellation/virtualization of FSUK 2020 dynamic events, which removed a full year of real-vehicle validation for that season's software.
long_lead_procurement: [uncertain] No specific week-level lead times were found for EUFS's sensors, actuators, or compute. Contextually relevant: the IMechE FS-AI FAQ notes that 'funding is available from the UK Government to assist UK teams with purchasing an ADS-DV platform,' implying the platform itself is a funded, non-trivial procurement, but no lead time in weeks is given.
first_dynamic_test_date: [uncertain] Not documented with a specific date; the closest data point is that the team had only ~3 days with the physical ADS-DV car before FSUK 2018 race week, suggesting the first dynamic test may have occurred essentially at or just before competition.
testing_hours_before_first_comp: [uncertain] Not documented; the '~3 days of familiarization before FSUK 2018' data point (Mapix, Jul 2018) is the only proxy available.
validation_strategy: Heavy reliance on eufs_sim (Gazebo) for pre-vehicle validation of perception/SLAM/planning/control before any physical laps. For the DDT/FS-AI class, using the shared ADS-DV platform additionally decoupled software validation risk from vehicle-build risk, since the vehicle itself was pre-built and rules-compliant.
rules_compliance_challenges: Achieving full ADS-class scrutineering (safety, technical, chassis, and accumulator all passing together) on their own-built vehicle has been the hardest bar for EUFS to clear - it was not achieved all at once; it came piecewise (technical+safety first passed 2024; chassis+accumulator first passed 2025), and 'complete scrutineering with an ADS vehicle' was still an explicit, unmet team goal going into FSUK 2026.
tech_inspection_experience: Did not pass scrutineering with their first self-built ADS-EV car (~2022) despite finishing the powertrain on schedule. Recovered incrementally: first passed technical and safety scrutineering with an ADS car in 2024 (a first in FSUK history for any team, per press coverage), then first passed chassis and accumulator scrutineering in 2025. Full combined scrutineering pass still not confirmed as of the 2026 SISU26 launch.
documentation_burden: [uncertain] Not documented with EUFS-specific detail beyond generic references to 'design reports' and static events common to all FS teams.
dv_event_results: 2018: 1st, DDT Class (inaugural win). 2019: 1st, DDT Class. 2020: [uncertain] ADS Class win claimed on team history page, but FSUK 2020 was a virtual/static-only event industry-wide (no live dynamics). 2021: 1st, ADS Class (whole FS-team best-ever placing of 21st that year). 2022: FS-AI class win continued (5th consecutive via DDT entry); separate self-built ADS-EV entry failed scrutineering. 2023: 1st, FS-AI class (6th consecutive); whole-team 21st in Concept Class. 2024: 1st, FS-AI class (7th consecutive), 822.1 points; first team in FSUK history to pass technical+safety scrutineering with an ADS car. 2025: 1st Overall FS-AI (8th consecutive win); won FS-AI Engineering Design, Track Drive, Skid Pad, Sprint, Endurance, and Overall Dynamic Events; joint 2nd in FS-AI Simulation Development; first year passing chassis+accumulator scrutineering. 2026: SISU26 launched 16 Mar 2026, targeting FSUK 2026 (15-19 Jul) and full ADS-vehicle scrutineering as a still-unmet goal.

reliability_notes: Self-built ADS-EV car failed scrutineering on its first competition entry (~2022) despite the powertrain being finished on schedule. No specific on-track DNF, cone-strike, or off-course incident data was found for the dominant DDT/FS-AI seasons (2018-2025).
top_mistakes: Per a former EUFS Driverless Software Team lead (2021-2023, siliconlad blog): trying to replicate the sophistication of teams that have '7 years' of experience within a single season typically fails; attempting to complete all dynamic events simultaneously instead of sequencing them ('If you try and complete all the events at the same time, you probably won't do any of them'); over-investing early in SLAM, global planning, expensive IMUs, or expensive LiDAR before they were actually needed ('You don't need SLAM. You don't need global planning. You don't need a fancy IMU, or an expensive LiDAR'); at the program level, EUFS also lost an entire season's real-vehicle validation to COVID in 2020, and their first self-built ADS-EV car failed scrutineering despite the powertrain finishing on time.
advice_for_new_teams: Direct quotes from a former EUFS Driverless Software Team lead (siliconlad.com/blog/how-to-fs-ai): 'Keep It Simple. Drill this into every member of your team. Then drill it in again.' Recommended event order to attack: Acceleration -> Autocross -> Trackdrive -> Skidpad. 'Don't waste your time trying to figure out how to do this yourselves' - i.e., use off-the-shelf integration libraries (he specifically recommends the `ros_can` library) rather than building custom CAN integration. 'Test the sh*t out of what you do have.' 'Learn to walk before you run.' He also recommends the ZED 2i stereo camera as a practical hardware choice and notes completing Acceleration+Autocross+Trackdrive alone is worth roughly 450 competition points.
team_structure_dv: Software side organized into Perception, Localisation & Mapping, Planning & Control, Software Infrastructure, Simulation, and Statics sub-groups. Mechanical side organized into Autonomous Hardware, Vehicle Dynamics, Chassis, and Aerodynamics & Ergonomics. Electrical side organized into Powertrain, PCB Design, Electrical Distribution Systems (EDS), and Control Systems (per eufs.co/driverless). Whole-team EUFS headcount grew from 10 founding members (2014) to over 170 by 2026; a 2020 first-hand account put the whole team at ~60 students with a total (not DV-specific) budget of over £70,000. The Driverless Software Team specifically has been led by a single lead for ~2-year terms in at least one documented case (2021-2023).
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: [uncertain] Not extensively documented. Available evidence: software leadership appears to run in multi-year terms (one documented lead served 2021-2023); the team relies on its own open-source simulator (eufs_sim) and GitLab CI/CD/documentation as onboarding tools, and produces public technical blog posts (siliconlad.com) as informal knowledge-transfer artifacts, but no formal onboarding process was documented.
budget_estimate: [uncertain] A 2020 first-hand account cites a whole-team (not DV-specific) budget of 'over £70,000'; no driverless-specific budget breakdown was found in any source.
recommended_sequence: Synthesized from EUFS's own history and alumni advice: 1) Acquire or borrow a spec, autonomous-ready platform (an ADS-DV equivalent) rather than building your own vehicle first, to remove vehicle-engineering risk from the driverless critical path. 2) Build the minimum viable perception + a simple pursuit-style controller sufficient for straight-line/low-speed events (Acceleration, then Autocross) before anything else. 3) Add stereo-camera fusion and EKF-based localization once basic autonomy is proven. 4) Only then layer in SLAM and MPC/global planning for Trackdrive, and treat Skidpad (which took EUFS ~4 years) as the hardest event to save for last. 5) Validate every change in simulation (eufs_sim/Gazebo) before every physical test. 6) Treat a fully self-built driverless vehicle (the 'ADS' class) as a genuine multi-year (5+ year) program, not a year-one goal - EUFS itself is still not fully through scrutineering on its own car after roughly 6 years of trying.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: EUFS's history is a strong argument for the requester's existing running EV to be treated the way EUFS treated its loaner ADS-DV: as the thing that removes vehicle-build risk from the 24-month critical path, letting the ~9 software-focused engineers focus entirely on the software sequence EUFS itself recommends (simple perception + pursuit control first, only adding SLAM/MPC/global planning later, one event at a time: Acceleration -> Autocross -> Trackdrive -> Skidpad). It also argues for realism: EUFS, with far more people (50-170+) and 8 years of unbroken class wins, still has not fully completed ADS-vehicle scrutineering on a from-scratch car as of 2026 - so a 24-month team should budget significant, sequenced time (not a single pass/fail milestone) for DT.3.2 EBS, DT.2.2 actuator decoupling, and DT.4 shutdown-circuit compliance, and should not assume that early competition success (which for EUFS came via a borrowed platform) implies the from-scratch build will be equally fast.
